idiom_name: single-owner access policy with hand-off or copy at thread boundaries (stack confinement, per-thread carrier, messages)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: decide the lifetime of the state, then bind it to the narrowest owner that covers that lifetime - a method's locals (stack confinement), a single task/actor (task confinement), or a thread (thread-local slot). Keep every reference private to the owner; the only sanctioned crossing is an explicit hand-off or copy (message, channel transfer, snapshot), never a shared live reference. Where the language offers a carrier (thread-local storage, per-task context), use it together with its cleanup protocol; where enforcement exists (ownership types, actor isolation), prefer it over convention. The classic locking structures remain justified when several threads genuinely must cooperate on long-lived state - there confinement is not applicable.
code_sketch:
owner = thread_or_task()            # exactly one
state  = new_non_thread_safe_state()
loop:
    request = owner.receive()       # hand-off or copy, never a shared reference
    state.mutate(request)           # no locks anywhere
# crossing threads:
next_owner <- message(copy_of_state)  # transfer, not share
pitfalls: Believing the language enforces confinement when only storage - not ownership - is checked; the first escaped pointer is a data race.
Choosing a per-thread slot for state that logically belongs to a request or task; pooled threads then carry it into unrelated work.
Confining the state but sharing a helper the state depends on (a static parser, a shared buffer) - the dependency is then the race.

Wrong move: capture confined state in a callback, listener or continuation scheduled on another thread -> how it fails: the owning thread and the callback thread now touch the object concurrently and the invariant silently breaks, usually in the rare timing the tests never hit -> instead hand the callback an immutable snapshot, or re-post the work back onto the owning thread (Handler.post, dispatch to the event loop, execute on the actor).

Wrong move: hand an object off through a shared queue or pool while the sender keeps using it or never clears its local reference -> how it fails: the transfer becomes a share with two simultaneous owners - which is exactly why sync.Pool's contract says the item belongs to the pool after Put -> instead nil out the reference at the moment of transfer and treat the object as gone.

Wrong move: treat 'the race detector saw nothing' as proof of confinement -> how it fails: detectors and escape analyses only judge executed paths, and formal work shows optimizations built on 'currently thread-local' evidence (partial lock elision) are unsound while race-check elision misses later races -> instead make ownership explicit (type-level non-sendable markers, thread-id assertions, static analysis) and re-audit every new call site that can reach the object.
